findings.problem: Every right-answer explanation opens the same way: a short cheer plus "baker!" ("There it is, baker!", "Yes, baker!" (Stop 1 Cards 4 and 10), "You nailed it, baker!", "Right on, baker!", "That's it, baker!", "Higher, baker!", "You got it, baker!", "Exactly, baker!", "YES, baker!", "Right you are, baker!", "Everlasting, baker!"). Nearly every missed-answer explanation says "friend" instead. That's a formula. These openers also work like a second right-answer reaction on top of the one the code already shows.

rule.text: There is no formula. Each explanation sounds natural and different from the others.

findings.problem: In the "delay" explanation, "Isaiah 55:1 opens with a call to \"you without money,\"" isn't accurate. The verse opens with "Come, all you who are thirsty, come to the waters". The call to "you without money" comes second.

rule.text: Noticing. What he points out must be true.

findings.problem: The "Abraham" explanation ends with "Right kind of promise, different name on it." That suggests God made Abraham a matching promise, which brings in another passage with no reference. Isaiah 55 says nothing about it.

rule.text: Connecting passages. When he connects two passages, or explains what a law was for, he says only what the texts state.

findings.problem: In the right-answer explanation, "These nations are running for GLORY" makes it sound like the nations run to get glory for themselves. Isaiah 55:5 says they run to the people because the LORD has bestowed glory on that people.

rule.text: Don't stretch the text. Exaggerate only in his own jokes.

findings.problem: The "False" explanation says "The wicked man forsakes his way and returns to the LORD", as if it really happened. In Isaiah 55:7 it's a call: "Let the wicked man forsake his way... let him return to the LORD".

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.

findings.problem: In the "everlasting" explanation, the joke "a sign that outlasts everything, including whatever I stamped on my first cookie" doesn't land. Why would his crooked first stamp be something that lasts? A reader has to stop and work it out.

rule.text: If a stranger would say "huh?", rewrite it.

findings.problem: Five explanations run 6 sentences, one more than the 3 to 5 the doc gives. Some of those sentences are one-word or one-line fragments: Stop 1 Card 4 "False", Stop 1 Card 10 "Their God has made them glorious", Stop 2 Card 3 "True", Stop 2 Card 8 "True" and "False".
findings.question: "About 3 to 5 sentences": do short fragments ("Never.", "Not halfway.", "No processing fee.") count as sentences, and is 6 allowed under "about"?

findings.problem: The "simpler" explanation makes up a one-time event: "I once spent twenty minutes looking for the spatula I was holding with my own mustache." Other cards have smaller made-up bakery bits too, like "I can't carry a tune past the mixing bowl" (Stop 2 Card 10) and a batch that "comes back as charcoal" (Stop 2 Card 8). papa-dorin.md says he "never adds anything new" to his backstory, family, bakery and mission. It also wants self-deprecating, laugh-out-loud jokes.
findings.question: Do throwaway self-deprecating jokes about his bakery or his habits count as "adding anything new" to the Dorinverse? Or are they allowed as personality, the way comparisons are?
